status: Original sample matns and shurūḥ for assessment; not yet integrated in canonical 1.8.0 edition
purpose: Capture the spiritual and emotional bearing of matching episodes in Martin Lings's Muhammad while retaining original prose, source distinction and explicit personal introductions. Attribution and bibliographic details are in the notes only.

examples.title: The household receives revelation
examples.matn:
As the years passed, periods of retreat at Ḥirāʾ drew Muḥammad ﷺ away from the business of Makkah. The solitude prepared a place of worship and attention amid the wider duties of life. In the cave he received the command to recite from the Lord who creates and teaches. The encounter overwhelmed him. He returned home shaken and asked Khadījah to cover him.

She received him within the security of a marriage in which she had learned the character of the man before her. She knew his truthfulness, hospitality, care for relatives and willingness to bear the burdens of vulnerable people. These were the grounds of her confidence as he recounted what had happened. Her reassurance joined the extraordinary event to the continuous reality of his life: the conduct she had witnessed now gave her reason to recognize the truth of the summons.

Khadījah then consulted her elderly cousin Waraqah, a man acquainted with earlier scripture. He recognized the likeness of the messenger of revelation known to previous prophets and warned of the opposition that such a mission would encounter. This recognition joined a household's intimate knowledge to the remembered history of revelation. The message was received through the Prophet's own experience; its initial shelter and witness arose within the relations of the household.

From that intimate beginning, recitation, worship and teaching gradually formed a circle of believers. The same person who received revelation would act as husband, father, teacher and guardian of a growing community. The inward gravity of revelation was carried into speech, affection, instruction and the difficult demands of allegiance.
examples.sharh:
The sequence is formative: retreat, revealed address, bodily awe, return to the household, intimate recognition and learned comparison with earlier prophecy. Each action has its own proper form. The received word originates in revelation. Its first communication is mediated by a person whose ordinary character is already known. The household supplies a relationship of confidence and care appropriate to the extraordinary event.[^1]

Revelatory receptivity becomes historically visible through the Prophet's return to a person who knows his sustained conduct. The event bears the structure of an integrated human life: spiritual disclosure is received through the body; the heart is overcome by awe; speech makes the encounter known; a spouse responds through the practical knowledge acquired over years. The character she describes concerns the vulnerable, kin, hospitality and the bearing of burdens. These are also the goods through which a larger community will later recognize rightful authority.

The household's recognition is one mode of response; the scripturally informed interpretation of an elder is another. Waraqah is relevant here because his place in Khadījah's kin network and familiarity with earlier prophetic texts supplies a distinguishable kind of testimony. His forewarning introduces a horizon of social opposition. The same revelation that entered a domestic setting now creates obligations that extend beyond that setting through teaching, communal life and public allegiance.[^2]

The wider principle is the movement from received divine address to an embodied life of service. The first scene gains its spiritual gravity from its human details: solitude and fear, the spouse's regard, a cloak, the known pattern of generosity and the first articulation of a future mission. Later teaching and legal disciplines preserve particular features of this beginning, while the personal unity of its original subject gives those features their coherence.[^3]

footnotes.text: **Primary witness.** [Al-Bukhārī 3](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3) reports the early revelations, the Prophet's return to Khadījah, her reassurance and the visit to Waraqah; Qurʾān 96:1–5 supplies the revealed opening. Compare variant chronology in the early Sīrah tradition.

**The witnesses.** The same report identifies Waraqah ibn Nawfal as Khadījah's relative and a reader of earlier religious texts. Later accounts vary in details; the explanatory distinction here concerns actual kinds of knowledge and relationships, not conjecture about his private spiritual rank.

**Narrative and emotional setting.** Martin Lings, *Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources*, chapters XII–XVI (particularly XV, “The First Revelations”), narrates the passage from solitude and awe to the shelter of Khadījah's household. This sample follows the episode's emotional proportions with independently composed prose and textual verification from Bukhārī 3.

examples.title: The painful treaty and the opening of peace
examples.matn:
When the Prophet ﷺ and his companions reached the approaches to Makkah intending pilgrimage, Quraysh prevented them from entering the sanctuary. The travellers had come in a state of devotion, yet the purpose of their journey now depended upon negotiation with those who had previously opposed them. The leaders of Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn ʿAmr to settle terms.

During the negotiations Suhayl's son Abū Jandal arrived seeking the Prophet's protection. He had embraced Islam and endured confinement in Makkah. His arrival brought the suffering of an individual believer into the middle of a treaty being negotiated between communities. The terms required the return of certain persons who fled Makkah; Suhayl insisted that his son be included. The Prophet met the painful claim within the obligations he was undertaking and reassured the young man concerning the relief God would provide.

The companions had travelled in hope of entering the sacred precinct. Their disappointment deepened when the agreement directed them to return without completing their intended visit. The Prophet commanded the sacrificial rites and the cutting of hair that would bring their state of consecration to a close. The men remained overcome by the situation. His wife Umm Salamah, who was accompanying the party, advised him to undertake the rites himself in their sight. He did so, and the companions followed.

The action gathered fidelity to a negotiated commitment, care for the distressed, the command to worship and attentive understanding of the companions' state. On the return journey, a revealed declaration named the agreement a clear victory. A peace whose immediate conditions had been difficult became a new setting for contact, instruction and alliances across Arabia.
examples.sharh:
The treaty brings unlike but simultaneous claims before one authority. The companions' sacred intention concerns worship; the agreement concerns reliable public obligation; Abū Jandal's arrival concerns an individual whose personal safety is immediately at stake; the party's subsequent hesitation concerns wounded expectation and the practical ability to respond to a command. The Prophet addresses these claims through speech, reassurance, agreement, counsel and embodied action.[^1]

Abū Jandal is central because his position cannot be reduced to a clause in an abstract text. He is the son of Suhayl, the Meccan negotiator, and a believer who had been constrained by his own people. His arrival makes the treaty's burden visible. The moral significance of the scene lies in the encounter of personal suffering, collective undertaking and confidence in an opening not yet visible. The transmitted negotiations also establish the political conditions within which later legal arguments about treaties could be formulated.

The companions' hesitation after the agreement raises another practical question: how can an authoritative instruction become effective when its recipients are distressed? Umm Salamah's counsel draws upon knowledge of the immediate human situation. The Prophet's performance of the sacrifice and hair-cutting gives a visible example that permits the others to follow. This is a union of right direction with the concrete pedagogical means by which it becomes operative.

Revelation then names the larger result. The truce allows contact and new instruction across previous lines of hostility, though each subsequent event requires its own historical evidence. The enduring lesson is a mode of practical judgment that relates an immediate claim to the end toward which worship, public trust and the formation of persons are directed.[^2]

footnotes.text: **Treaty and persons.** [Al-Bukhārī 2731–2732](https://sunnah.com/bukhari/54/19) records the negotiations, Suhayl, Abū Jandal, the companions' difficulty and Umm Salamah's counsel. The accounts require careful distinction between the reported legal terms and later juristic generalizations.

**Emotional movement and narrative pacing.** Martin Lings, *Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources*, chapters LXVI–LXVIII (“The Dilemma of Quraysh,” “A Clear Victory” and “After Hudaybiyah”), draws attention to the tension between disappointment, action and the eventual broader meaning of the treaty. Qurʾān 48:1 and 48:18 anchor the revealed language of victory and the pledge.
